title: The Jarl's Dashboard
subject: Business analytics
intro: The Jarl wants one clear view of how the island's trade is doing. Sort the measures into a dashboard and explain what they mean together.

objectives.label: Explain what makes a measure a KPI
Group KPIs into revenue, profitability and customer experience
Interpret KPIs together, not one at a time
Choose a suitable chart for a KPI

badge.name: Hall Analyst
badge.description: Organised KPIs into a dashboard and read them together.

takeaway: A KPI is a measure tied to a goal and tracked over time. Group KPIs by the question they answer, and read them together: growing sales with a shrinking margin tells a different story from either number alone.

scenes.title: The Great Hall
scenes.speaker: astrid
lines: Welcome to the Great Hall, Pathfinder. The Jarl is drowning in numbers.
Every trader sends a different report. He wants one dashboard: a few key measures, clearly grouped.
Help me build it, and help me explain what it says.

scenes.title: What is a KPI?
scenes.speaker: astrid
scenes.context: KPI stands for Key Performance Indicator.
scenes.prompt: Which description best fits a KPI?

options.text: A measure linked to a goal, tracked over time to show progress
options.feedback: Yes. "Key" means it matters to a goal; "indicator" means it shows how things are going.
Businesses record thousands of numbers. A KPI is one of the few that shows progress towards a goal.

options.text: The biggest number on the report
options.feedback: Size doesn't make a number important. A small percentage can matter more than a large total.
Many KPIs aren't money: satisfaction scores and delivery times are KPIs too.

hints: Think about the word "key". Key to what?
A good KPI tells you whether you're getting closer to something you want.
scenes.explanation: KPIs are the handful of measures that show whether you're meeting your goals. Everything else is supporting detail.

scenes.title: Learn: grouping KPIs on a dashboard
scenes.speaker: astrid

lesson.objective: Group measures by the business question they answer.
lesson.plainEnglish: A dashboard shows a few key measures (KPIs) at a glance. It is easier to read when KPIs are grouped by the question they answer. Three common groups are revenue (money coming in, and whether it’s growing), profitability (what’s left after costs), and customer experience (how customers feel and behave).
lesson.analogy: A car dashboard: speed, fuel and engine warnings each have their own place, so you know where to look.

example.code:
A gym's dashboard
Revenue:        membership income · new sign-ups this month
Profitability:  cost per member · profit margin
Customers:      class satisfaction · members renewing
example.caption: Different business, same three questions.

lesson.whyItMatters: Grouped KPIs let decision-makers answer “are we selling, are we keeping money, are customers happy?” in seconds.
lesson.commonMistake: Grouping numbers by where they came from (which spreadsheet or team) instead of the question they answer.
lesson.takeaway: For each KPI, ask: money in, money kept, or customer experience?

scenes.title: Build the dashboard
scenes.speaker: astrid
scenes.context: Here are nine measures from the traders' reports.
scenes.prompt: Place each KPI card into the dashboard section that it helps answer.

categories.label: Revenue & growth
categories.description: How much are we selling, and is it growing?

categories.label: Profitability
categories.description: Do we keep money after costs?

categories.label: Customer experience
categories.description: Are customers happy and coming back?

cards.label: Total sales this month
cards.feedback: Total sales measures money coming in: revenue.

cards.label: Sales growth vs last month
cards.feedback: Growth compares revenue between periods, so it belongs with revenue.

cards.label: Average order value
cards.feedback: Average order value is revenue divided by orders, a revenue measure.

cards.label: Gross profit margin
cards.feedback: Margin is the share of each sale kept after the cost of goods: profitability.

cards.label: Cost per order
cards.feedback: Costs drive profitability: what you keep depends on what you spend.

cards.label: Net profit
cards.feedback: Net profit is money left after all costs, the core profitability measure.

cards.label: Customer satisfaction score
cards.feedback: Satisfaction comes from customers' own ratings, so it measures customer experience.

cards.label: Repeat-customer rate
cards.feedback: Customers returning is a sign of a good experience.

cards.label: Average delivery time
cards.feedback: Delivery speed is something customers feel directly: customer experience.

scenes.successFeedback: Three clear sections, three KPIs each.
hints: Ask of each card: is it about money in, money kept, or how customers feel?
Margin, costs and profit are all about what's left after spending.
scenes.explanation: Grouping KPIs by the question they answer makes a dashboard readable at a glance: are we selling, are we keeping money, are customers happy?

scenes.title: Reading KPIs together
scenes.speaker: astrid
scenes.context: This month, sales grew 8%, but gross profit margin fell from 45% to 42%.
scenes.prompt: What should the dashboard tell the Jarl?

options.text: We're selling more, but keeping less of each sale. Look at what has pushed costs up
options.feedback: Yes. Read together, the two KPIs point to a cost problem hidden behind good sales news.

options.text: Sales are up 8%, so everything is going well
options.feedback: Growth alone hides the falling margin. Each sale now earns less.

options.text: Margin is down, so the business is failing
options.feedback: That's too strong. Sales are growing, and 42% may still be healthy. It's a warning to investigate, not a verdict.

options.text: Report only the good number to keep the Jarl happy
options.feedback: A dashboard that hides bad news can't support good decisions.

hints: What does each number say on its own? What do they say together?
If you sell more but keep a smaller share, what has probably changed?
scenes.explanation: KPIs make the most sense side by side. Growth with a falling margin often means costs or discounts are rising, which is worth investigating before it erodes profit.

lesson.objective: Match a chart type to the question being asked.
lesson.plainEnglish: Match the chart to the question. For change over time, use a line chart. To compare categories, use a bar chart. For parts of a whole with only a few parts, use a pie or stacked bar. For one headline number, use a big number card.
lesson.analogy: Choosing a map: a road map for driving and a tube map for the Underground. Both are maps, but each answers a different question.

example.code:
Question                               Chart
Which shop sold the most?              Bar chart
What share of orders came online?      Pie or stacked bar (few parts)
How many members do we have today?     Big number card

lesson.whyItMatters: The right chart makes the answer obvious; the wrong one hides it.
lesson.commonMistake: A pie chart with many similar slices, which makes differences almost impossible to see.
lesson.takeaway: Time → line, compare → bar, share → pie (few parts), headline → number.

scenes.title: Choosing a chart
scenes.speaker: astrid
scenes.context: The Jarl wants to see how monthly sales changed over the past year.

options.text: A line chart with months along the bottom
options.feedback: Yes. Lines are made for change over time: rises, dips and trends are visible at a glance.

options.text: A pie chart with one slice per month
options.feedback: Pie charts show parts of a whole. Twelve similar slices make trends almost impossible to see.
A table is precise, but readers have to work to spot the trend. A chart shows it immediately.

options.text: One big number showing the yearly total
options.feedback: A total hides how sales changed month to month, which is what the Jarl asked.

hints: The question is about change over time.
Which chart joins points in order from left to right?
scenes.explanation: Match the chart to the question: line charts for trends over time, bar charts for comparing categories, and big single numbers for headline KPIs.

scenes.title: The dashboard is ready
scenes.speaker: astrid
lines: Nine measures, three clear questions, and an honest story about what they mean together.
The Jarl will finally see the island at a glance, the good news and the warnings.
You've walked every trail on this island, Pathfinder. The Atlas grows because of you.
